slides.title: Two guesses from 7,002 bitcoin

items: 2011: paid 7,002 BTC for an animated bitcoin explainer
Keys on an encrypted drive; password on a paper, lost
The drive allows ten guesses - by 2021, eight were gone
Front page of the New York Times, and of this chapter

items.who: Stefan Thomas, programmer (early bitcoin adopter, later Ripple's CTO)
items.where: an IronKey USB drive in a safe - and the front page of the New York Times

slides.notes:
STORY (2021-01-12): In 2011 Stefan Thomas was paid 7,002 BTC for making an animated explainer about bitcoin. He put the keys on an encrypted IronKey drive, wrote the password on a paper he later lost, and the drive allows ten guesses before locking forever. By January 2021, when the New York Times told the story, he had used eight. The chapter you are in - recovery codes, written backups, backup TESTING - is the discipline that makes this story impossible to repeat.
SOURCE: The New York Times, 2021-01-12, 'Lost Passwords Lock Millionaires Out of Their Bitcoin Fortunes': 7,002 BTC, ten guesses, eight used. Photo: Lift Conference 2015, CC BY 2.0 (the file page names Stefan Thomas).
slides.take: Memory is not a backup - this chapter is the alternative

items.label: same seed in, same keys out - always

slides.notes:
SAY: Independent key generation is the method in which a wallet application creates each of the keys that it plans to use independently of the others. Each is a fresh random number with no connection to the rest, and the wallet database is simply the collection of them.

slides.title: Recovery codes
slides.sub: Entropy, dressed for handwriting

items.cap: entropy to code - Mastering Bitcoin 3e, CC BY-SA

slides.notes:
SAY: A recovery code is the short, written form of a wallet's seed: a sequence of words, or in one case a string of letters and digits, from which every key of a deterministic wallet can be computed again.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - RecoveryCodes.

slides.title: Twelve words between you and 128 bits

items.cap: Trezor One devices - photo: Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0

items: 2013: the first hardware-wallet team hits a human problem
Nobody transcribes 128 raw bits correctly
BIP 39: 2,048 words, 11 bits each, checksum folded in
These slides run that standard against its own vectors

items.who: Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak (SatoshiLabs/Trezor), with Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe
items.where: BIP 39, in the public bips repository

slides.notes:
STORY (2013-09-10): The team building the first hardware signing device faced a human problem: nobody transcribes 128 raw bits correctly. Their 2013 proposal, BIP 39, encodes entropy as ordinary words from a curated list of 2,048 - eleven bits a word, a checksum folded in, a key-stretching function from words to seed. The slides around this one do not describe that pipeline; they run it, word by word, against the standard's own test vectors.
SOURCE: BIP 39, 'Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys', authors Palatinus, Rusnak, Voisine, Bowe, dated 2013-09-10, in bitcoin/bips. Photo: two Trezor One devices by Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0.
slides.take: The recovery code is an interface between humans and entropy

slides.title: Words to bits, measured
slides.sub: The whole size table, computed - then checked word by word

items.title: Entropy carried by a recovery code (bits)

slides.notes:
SAY: The length of a recovery code is not a free choice: it is determined by the amount of entropy. The chapter prints the relation as a table with four columns, entropy in bits, checksum in bits, entropy plus checksum, and recovery code words, whose five rows run from 128 bits and 12 words to 256 bits and 24 words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why eleven bits a word - what is 2 to the 11?

slides.take: Eleven bits a word; the checksum rides along

slides.title: From words to seed, slowly on purpose
slides.sub: PBKDF2, salt, and the passphrase that changes everything

items.label: same words, new passphrase - different wallet

rows: TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'
items.label: the stretcher itself - and it refuses sloppy input

slides.notes:
SAY: PBKDF2 is the second password-based key derivation function of the PKCS #5 standard, and it is the particular key-stretching function BIP39 names. Its specification defines it as applying a pseudorandom function to derive keys, with four inputs: a password, a salt, an iteration count and the intended length of the derived key in octets, and says it is recommended for new applications (Moriarty et al., 2017).
ASK: Where must the passphrase NOT be stored - and why is 'nowhere' a defensible answer?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - Pbkdf2, RecoveryPassphrase.
slides.take: The passphrase changes everything - by design

slides.title: The tree and its paths
slides.sub: One seed, a numbered key for every purpose
slides.notes:
SAY: A hierarchical deterministic wallet, which the chapter and the standards abbreviate to HD wallet, is a wallet whose keys form a tree, every node of which is computed from the seed. The book's glossary calls the hierarchical deterministic protocol the key creation and transfer protocol of BIP32, which allows creating child keys from parent keys in a hierarchy, and an HD wallet a wallet using that protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - HdWallet.

slides.title: One seed, a tree of keys
slides.sub: HMAC-SHA512 splits every node in two

items: The seed makes a master key and a chain code
Each child: HMAC of parent and an index
32 bytes of key, 32 of chain code - every node

items.label: the master pair, derived and range-checked
child zero, with its own chain code

slides.notes:
SAY: Hierarchical deterministic key generation, usually shortened to HD, is the standard way to derive keys from a seed. It is defined in BIP32, a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal by Pieter Wuille that has the status Deployed (Wuille, 2012).
ASK: Why carry a chain code at all - what would leak without it?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - HdKeyGeneration, ChildKeyDerivation.
slides.take: Two 32-byte halves at every node keep the tree alive

slides.title: The paths everyone agreed on
slides.sub: Five levels, and Core derives the same address we do

items.label: purpose / coin / account / change / index - hardened where it matters
BIP-84's own test vector: our math, then Core's answer - equal

items: 44h legacy
49h nested
84h segwit
86h taproot

slides.notes:
SAY: BIP44 is the layout that gives a tree its familiar shape. The chapter says that, extending BIP43, BIP44 proposes a multi-account structure as purpose number 44 with a prime, that all wallets following the structure are identified by using only the branch m/44', and that the structure consists of five predefined tree levels: purpose, coin type, account, change and address index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Your phone wallet says 'account 0' - write its path from memory.

slides.title: The 200,000 BTC in a forgotten wallet file

items.label: reported found, three weeks into bankruptcy
when the old-format wallet file was last used
later, those coins began repaying creditors

items: A file written by software two generations older still held spendable keys
Backups do not expire - label them, test them, never discard them blindly

items.who: Mt. Gox, weeks into its bankruptcy proceedings
items.where: an old-format wallet file, unused since June 2011

slides.notes:
STORY (2014-03-21): Chapter 1 told how Mt. Gox collapsed owing 850,000 BTC. Three weeks after the bankruptcy filing came a twist: the company reported finding about 200,000 BTC in an old-format wallet file that had sat unused since 2011. A file made by software two generations older still held spendable keys - backups do not expire. Those coins became the pool from which creditors, a decade later, began to be repaid.
SOURCE: Mt. Gox announcement of 2014-03-20/21 reporting approximately 200,000 BTC found in an old-format wallet; summarized with the bankruptcy chronology at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Gox.
slides.take: Backups do not expire - treat old wallet files as live keys

slides.title: Split the secret, not the risk
slides.sub: Shamir: three of five recovers; two learn nothing

items: Split the seed into five shares, threshold three
Any three reconstruct it exactly
Any two: provably nothing - the run shows both

items.label: SLIP-39 does this in words; Codex32 by hand on paper

slides.notes:
SAY: Secret sharing is a way of splitting one secret into several parts with a threshold. SLIP39's description is the clearest: the scheme splits a secret into a number of unique parts, of which any threshold-many are required to reconstruct it, and knowledge of fewer than the required number does not leak information about the secret (Rusnak et al., 2017).
ASK: Where do five shares live so no burglary, flood, or sibling feud collects three?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - SecretSharing, Slip39Code.
slides.take: Three of five recovers; two of five learns nothing
